text.p: Continental Airlines and Northwest Airlines said they still had no plans to drop cargo fuel surcharges despite a decision by Deutsche Lufthansa AG to do so next Tuesday.
It was not immediately known how other large North American carriers, notably American Airlines, would be influenced by Lufthansa's decision.
Airlines that have dropped the surcharge include United Airlines, Virgin Atlantic and Delta Airlines.
Dutch shippers told Reuters this week that KLM, Northwest's marketing partner, is also expected to drop its surcharge on April 15.
Lufthansa Cargo was the first major carrier to introduce a fuel surcharge last November to deal with soaring fuel prices.
In recent weeks, fuel prices have staged a partial retreat, though most carriers say they remain above year-ago levels.
Lufthansa now says its fuel prices have receded to July 1996 levels.
In the U.S., the airlines say fuel is not back down to July 1996 levels let alone October 1996 peak levels.
"We're not in a position yet (with respect to) our fuel purchasing where we can lift our fuel surcharge," said Dana Bates, Continental's manager of cargo marketing.

Market sources say that Continental was one of last year's most aggressive fuel hedgers when prices were rising, but its current hedge may also be negating part of the benefit of falling prices. Also, jet fuel prices in the U.S. have not fallen as fast as the underlying crude price.

Northwest is a major freighter operator in the U.S.-Asia market but is a smaller player on the North Atlantic, where it sells strictly belly space. So far, none of the major Asian carriers has joined United in dropping the surcharge, making the transpacific market the most prominent holdout against dropping the surcharge.
